webTitle: Trump homeland security chief says ICE agents could be sent to polling places

fields.headline: Trump homeland security chief says ICE agents could be sent to polling places
fields.trailText: Markwayne Mullin says officers could be deployed ‘if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant’
fields.bodyText: The US homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, on Tuesday said that federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country. Speaking to reporters in New York, Mullin said: “ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places. We’re there to enforce specific threats.” For months, Democrats and voting rights groups have warned that the Trump administration might attempt to deploy federal agents to polling locations in an effort to intimidate voters and depress turnout ahead of the November midterm elections. Although the White House has downplayed such suggestions, Donald Trump has declined to rule it out while continuing to sow doubt about the integrity of past – and future – US elections. “The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. That’s their job … if we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.” Federal law prohibits military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held”. In a separate statement to Politico, the homeland security department said: “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.” The Guardian has contacted the DHS for additional comment. Mullin’s latest comments follow statements he made in July, when he threatened to withhold federal aid from states that refused to comply with homeland security election directives as part of the administration’s crackdown on what it alleges is widespread voter fraud. “We will scrub all election records, looking for illegal aliens and those who are ineligible to vote, including those that somehow voted, yet they were deceased,” Mullin said earlier this summer, adding: “If states want the grant funding, to recap, they must secure the election.” Yet experts say the administration has failed to offer any proof for its claims of non-citizen voting. In one instance, the DHS officials claimed that there may have been as many as 16,000 non-citizens registered to vote in Nevada, but later admitted they could confirm that only 185 of those people were actually non-citizens, according to records obtained by the Guardian. Meanwhile, Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff, recently wrote in a letter that the US military had no plans to deploy troops to polling sites during the upcoming November midterm elections. Caine’s letter came in response to a request for information from Senator Elissa Slotkin amid concerns that the Trump administration could send US military personnel to patrol polling sites. In his letter to Slotkin, Caine said: “The joint force has no plans to send federal military personnel or federalized members of the national guard to polling places during the 2026 elections.” He added that there were “no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material”.

webTitle: House passes funding bill to avoid shutdown before midterms

fields.headline: House passes funding bill to avoid shutdown before midterms
fields.trailText: Continuing resolution to approve government spending until 11 December passes 370-48 and will now go to Trump
fields.bodyText: The US House of Representatives on Tuesday approved legislation to prevent a government shutdown through the midterms, as both parties opted to defuse a volatile dispute before the November elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. A continuing resolution (CR) authorizing government spending until 11 December passed the House by a 370-48 vote, with only 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats in opposition. Had it not passed, lawmakers would have had until the end of September to approve new funding or face a government shutdown. The measure, which keeps federal spending at their current levels until the CR expires, now heads to Trump’s desk, after the Senate approved it last month by an overwhelming margin. In July, the House passed its own CR that would have authorized government spending until 4 December, but most Democrats rejected it for funding immigration enforcement agencies without including new guardrails on their conduct that they had demanded, and the Senate never took it up. The relatively uneventful end to the annual government funding debate comes as lawmakers step up their campaigning before the 3 November elections, in which most forecasters believe Democratic candidates have an edge in retaking the majority in the House of Representatives. There are mounting signs that the minority may also be able to regain control of the Senate by winning seats in at least three states that voted for Trump two years ago, as the president struggles with approval ratings driven lower by persistent inflation and the war with Iran. In the run-up to the vote, top House Democrats said they were ready to support the Senate measure, noting it included policy tweaks that the party supported. Among those was a delay until 11 December on a new rule by the White House office of management and budget that Democrats feared would allow the Trump administration to cancel grants at any time for any reason. “Given that the objectives that we had were met, I think that there’s going to be broad bipartisan support,” Pete Aguilar, the Democratic caucus chair, told reporters before the vote. Tensions flared among House Democrats later on Tuesday, when representatives Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington unexpectedly joined Republicans to help House speaker Mike Johnson pass a procedural rule governing debate on a suite of GOP-backed bills. The Democrats’ votes effectively salvaged Johnson’s agenda in the face of a conservative revolt that risked tanking Republicans’ legislative priorities. While Golden, who is retiring at the end of his term, and Gluesenkamp Perez, who is running for re-election in a district Trump won in 2024, often buck their party, the move was highly unusual and prompted a sharp rebuke from Democratic leadership. In a joint statement, Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, whip Katherine Clark and Aguilar said the two lawmakers had “blindside[d] the entire House Democratic Caucus” and called their actions a “significant breach of trust”. “It is an action that necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order,” they said. Passage of the rule paved the way on Tuesday for a vote on a resolution denouncing socialism in “all its forms”, which passed the divided chamber with the support of Republicans and eight Democrats. Tuesday’s floor action was a reminder of the deep divisions within the Democratic ranks after losing control of both houses of Congress in the 2024 elections. Without power in Congress, they have used the Senate’s filibuster to force the government closed and push the Republican majority into compromising over their preferred policies. Last year, Senate Democrats instigated a government shutdown by refusing to vote for any spending bill that did not extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later. Some government agencies shut down again briefly earlier this year after Democrats held up a funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in protest of the killings by federal agents of two US citizens in Minneapolis during an intensive immigration enforcement drive. While an agreement was reached to resolve that blockade, the two parties did not agree on funding the DHS for weeks, as Democrats held out for reforms to immigration enforcement operations. A bipartisan agreement was reached to fund the department operations exclusive of the agencies involved in Trump’s mass deportation push; then Republicans passed a party-line bill that allocated funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection for the duration of Trump’s presidency, with no reforms to immigration enforcement.

webTitle: New system for screening mail-in ballots risks denying entire batches, says whistleblower

fields.headline: New system for screening mail-in ballots risks denying entire batches, says whistleblower
fields.trailText: US senator says that project, a key part of Trump’s voting restrictions, is ‘perilously rushed and potentially unlawful’
fields.bodyText: A new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for this November’s US midterm elections was thrown together so hastily, and tested so little, that a single scanning glitch could see entire batches of ballots turned away, a whistleblower has told Congress. The project – a key part of Donald Trump’s new restrictions on voting – is “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to the US senator Richard Blumenthal, who disclosed the warning in a letter to David Steiner, the postmaster general, on Tuesday. Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the US Senate’s permanent subcommittee on investigations, said the account he had received made clear the US Postal Service “lacks the technical or operational capability” to roll it out safely before ballots go out to voters. The system stems from a March executive order by Trump tightening federal control over mail-in voting, directing USPS to check ballots against a federally approved voter list before sending them – a break from its usual role of simply delivering whatever is handed over by states. Courts have blocked and unblocked parts of the order repeatedly since, amid lawsuits arguing it oversteps into territory the constitution leaves to states. USPS calls the result the “Federal Ballot Mail Portal”. Officials upload voter and barcode data in advance; clerks then scan a sample of arriving ballots – 15 to 400, depending on batch size – against that list. According to the whistleblower’s disclosure, the system runs on a “zero percent failure rate”: one mismatched scan rejects the entire batch, even if it holds tens of thousands of ballots. USPS was contacted for comment. Engineers had roughly three months, including a court-ordered pause, for work the whistleblower says would normally take close to a year. The full system was not even assembled for testing until about 24 August, the disclosure says, leaving only a handful of working days to catch problems before launch. By the final week, officials were reportedly calling the effort “a shit show”, and one worker who raised concerns about the lack of testing time was told simply: “We cannot fail.” About a third of voters cast ballots by mail in 2024. The whistleblower’s prediction of mass disruption remains unconfirmed – the system had not gone live as of this week. “The whistleblower’s allegations make clear that USPS lacks the technical or operational capability needed to effectively implement the EO’s [executive order’s] provisions in a way that safeguards every citizen’s right to vote in the upcoming midterm elections,” Blumenthal wrote. “Despite this, the Trump Administration appears intent on USPS moving forward with its flawed plans, no matter the chaos they may create.” Blumenthal’s letter also alleges USPS kept building the portal under active court orders to stop, including one issued on 27 August that remains in force. “USPS should have ceased all work on the Portal on June 25, 2026,” he wrote. Blumenthal has given USPS until 4 September to answer questions, including who ordered the work to begin and resume, and until 8 September to hand over internal records. USPS has not disclosed an expected rejection rate, which the whistleblower says was withheld because it would expose how shaky the rollout is. The representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, said his panel had received similar reports. “This new secret tracking system at the US Postal Service is faulty, untested, and threatens to totally disrupt ballot delivery for millions of American citizens,” Garcia said, calling the policy an “unconstitutional and dangerous power grab”.

webTitle: What should we do with Trump’s monstrous architectural legacy? | Jan-Werner Müller

fields.headline: What should we do with Trump’s monstrous architectural legacy?
fields.trailText: Questions over Trump’s ballroom and other structures might not feel urgent. But when his reign ends, Trumpism must be repudiated
fields.bodyText: On Monday, a majority on the supreme court found a technical way to overrule a lower court’s imperative to stop work, while not taking a stance on whether the whole enterprise might be illegal to begin with. Preservationists, the majority held, appear to lack legal grounds for filing a suit blocking Trump’s ballroom; that means construction will proceed, even if none other than John Roberts, in a dissent, held that “those responsible” were breaking the rules in deciding “what to build up at the People’s House”. The solicitor general, John Sauer, is on record claiming that 65% of the project is completed (of course, he might have exaggerated – such things are known to have happened in Trump administrations). Either way, it is thus likely that there will be a massive structure next to the original White House; and, given that the ruling will embolden the president dramatically to change Washington DC’s landscape by spending money never approved by Congress, we might be cursed with a triumphal arch as well. All of which raises the question: what to do with a monstrous architectural legacy in post-Trump America? Some might dismiss the question as a bit of a luxury problem. After all, a war that also demonstrates the ongoing disempowerment of Congress keeps dragging on; ICE continues its cruel day-to-day work; Trump is trying every tactic to make the midterms go his way. But the built environment, and especially the civic landscape of a capital, is never just an afterthought. Buildings and monuments make values visible, as the philosopher Susan Neiman once put it. And the decision to leave Trump’s structures in place as if his reign had just been another normal era in US history is not neutral – just like leaving Confederate monuments in place is not neutral. For those who dismiss talk of civic values made visible as all too idealistic, there is another, hard-nosed argument to consider: after all, for anyone around the globe ever to trust a US government again, Trumpism will need to be thoroughly repudiated. Without a clear distancing from his toxic reign – during which the whims and obsessions of one evidently incompetent conman wreaked havoc with old alliances – other countries might well conclude that the US has failed to learn any lessons. And the built environment is a prime candidate for making that distancing visible to the outside world. The ballroom in particular has become a central symbol of Trump 2.0, as it combines core features of Trump’s governance: the shameless corruption, as private companies are invited to “donate” for the project; the sheer destructiveness, as the East Wing was brutally torn down without discussion, let alone permission – something that Trumpists might try to repeat with the Kennedy Center, as Howard Lutnick and others are threatening that it will have to be demolished unless Trump gets to “renovate” and have his name on it (notice the abuser’s logic of “if I cannot have it, no one can have it”). Democrats, noticing the symbolic importance of the structure, have started to weigh in on its future: Gavin Newsom, the California governor, affirming that “we have to be builders” and not destroyers, would just leave things alone; Senator Chris Murphy has suggested that all “dirty” – which seems to mean: corrupt – projects under Trump might need to go; meanwhile, Senator Ruben Gallego wants to sell the ballroom off “piece by piece” (it is unclear whether that would be some sort of political performance art, intended as a comment on corruption, or an act of symbolic catharsis, copying the way people demolished the Berlin wall piece by piece). The prior, fundamental question is whether a structure honors a particular person or at least affirms a set of political values. This was always the strongest reason why monuments of those defending slavery could simply not be left standing; as Neiman also pointed out, there was no way a Germany that still had Hitler street names – let alone Hitler statues – could have regained the trust of anyone. So, as painful as it might be for members of the Maga cult, no official building should bear Trump’s name, and no publicly funded statues of him must ever be erected – unless the country decides that we should honor a man bent on establishing autocracy in the US. Then again, some republics have precisely not erased all traces of a tyrannical ruler because they wanted such traces to serve as a warning to future generations. Visitors to Venice’s most famous palace can marvel at portraits of all the doges, except one that is painted over with a black shroud; here the dishonor of the person – Doge Marino Faliero, who attempted a coup – is immortalized, and the moral meaning of history unmistakably clarified. Political iconoclasm wants to leave remnants of an image in place to remind people why iconoclasm had been necessary in the first place. That is why some have suggested that problematic monuments should ideally not be removed at all, but come with explicit statements, such as plaques that disavow their initial political message – or even be legitimately vandalized, such that both original and acts of vandalism remain clearly visible. Contextualization has a pedagogical impulse similar to that of museums; hence, there is something coherent about the congressman Jamie Raskin and the progressive politician Saikrat Chakrabarti suggesting the ballroom should at least partly be turned into exhibition spaces documenting corruption, autocracy and what Raskin described as attempts to “undermine and thwart popular democracy in American life” (though, as Raskin seeks to keep a space for dining, too, guests might end up awkwardly sipping champagne next to depictions of January 6). Perhaps there is a more straightforward approach: the edifice could be named after Renee Good and Alex Pretti, the way some places in the south ended up testifying to those who fought injustice. This could teach a history lesson in a way that, for instance, turning the ballroom into a soup kitchen, as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has suggested, might not – worthy as that idea might also appear. Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University

webTitle: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election

fields.headline: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election
fields.trailText: Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago
fields.bodyText: The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard. Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest. “There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy. More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfather was murdered by the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election. October’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup. Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula. The US measures include imposing 25% tariffs on most Brazilian imports and designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – as foreign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime. In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, who reportedly planned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington was revoked. Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media. “The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.” Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared. Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their book Brazil: A Biography. Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.” Green sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil. But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.” The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement. “We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.” Last year Trump was accused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentina after he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”. Green believes two strategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project. Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimise Lula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba. Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamed Latin America’s “orange wave”. Paiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence. Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”. He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted “the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros” had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term. Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags. Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”. “The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.

webTitle: House Republicans ramp up labor union investigations before midterms

fields.headline: House Republicans ramp up labor union investigations before midterms
fields.trailText: Inquiries come after conservative thinktanks claim unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes
fields.bodyText: House Republicans are investigating several US labor unions based on claims from far-right non-profits alleging union dues are being used for illegal political funding. Republicans on the House’s education and workforce committee opened the investigation this summer after multiple reports from the conservative thinktanks targeted unions and their spending, claiming that unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes. While unions are allowed to advocate for political causes, they are prohibited from using union dues to directly fund specific candidates or political action committees (Pacs). Union members can voluntarily donate to labor unions’ political action committees. The unions under investigation include the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), United Auto Workers, United Steelworkers, Smart Transportation Division (Smart-TD), Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen (BLET), and the Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees Division (BMWED). The allegations come from research reports by the American Accountability Foundation (AAF), a “dark money” non-profit that counts Project 2025 architect the Heritage Foundation as a donor, and the Freedom Foundation, a conservative thinktank whose chair once protested against Labor Day, claiming: “I can’t think of a problem in society that can’t be traced in some way back to the abuses of organized labor.” Among the AAF’s allegations against labor unions are that the BLET supported a lawsuit filed by the UAW to halt the Trump administration’s attempt to end collective bargaining. It also highlighted the BLET’s criticism of Project 2025, which advocates for several policies that would weaken labor unions and collective bargaining rights. “The industrial unions the [House] committee is investigating have become glorified political arms of the Democrat Party,” said Tom Jones, president of the American Accountability Foundation in a statement. “When these unions care more about their friends in Congress than their members in the factories and railroads, it becomes clear they’re not serving the working men and women of America!” In a statement, a spokesperson for United Steelworkers said the group is “working diligently on fully addressing the committee’s request”. “Our union values transparency and annually reports our spending with the Department of Labor,” the spokesperson said. As a part of their union investigations, House Republicans are also investigating AFT president Randi Weingarten after the Freedom Foundation claimed, using speculation around the union’s annual financial filing, that union member dues funded her 2025 book, Why Fascists Fear Teachers: Public Education and the Future of Democracy. “Perhaps Weingarten’s next book should be entitled, Why Teachers Fear Teachers Unions,” the analysis claimed. In a letter responding to the allegations, Michael Bromwich, an attorney representing Weingarten and the AFT, called the Freedom Foundation’s report “a partisan attack masquerading as investigative journalism”. “Its claims are premised on factual inaccuracies, misleading characterizations, and a willful disregard for the complete record,” Bromwich wrote. “The documents produced to the House committee refute these allegations and demonstrate that the book project was lawfully and ethically undertaken to advance AFT’s mission, with appropriate oversight and transparent financial arrangements.” The Freedom Foundation and House Republicans on the investigating committee did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The House investigations follow reports that the Trump administration conducted surveillance of labor unions in Minnesota during a mass anti-immigration enforcement operation earlier this year, including the CWA and the SEIU. Cathy Creighton, director of Cornell University’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations Buffalo Co-Lab, said that union finances are strictly controlled, with disclosure requirements on how money is spent – which is how the conservative groups got the information for their reports. Most union members vote Democrat, because the party “has a platform that supports the labor movement, the right to organize [and] the right to bargain”, Creighton said. “The labor movement is allowed to spend money on political actions, and they do,” she said, noting that the motivation behind the reports seemed political. “The Trump administration has been trying to eliminate bargaining rights and unions, full stop.” A 2024 poll by Gallup found that 62% of Americans say the Democratic party best serves the interest of union members compared with 27% who said the same about the Republican party. US labor unions have historically supported Democrats over Republicans since Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s administration passed the National Labor Relations Act in 1935. But Republican presidents, up until Ronald Reagan in the 1980s, refrained from taking hostile positions toward labor unions and collective bargaining. In 1976, Republican Gerald Ford’s presidential campaign stated “free collective bargaining remains the best way to insure that American workers receive a fair price for their labors”. But under Reagan, the Republican party began to emphasize so-called “right to work” laws over collective bargaining and adopted more hostile, pro-business stances toward labor unions. Under Trump’s second term, he issued an executive order to rescind collective bargaining rights from more than 1 million federal workers and made cuts to federal agencies tasked with enforcing labor laws.

webTitle: Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster | Michael Mann

fields.headline: Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster
fields.trailText: The deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action now
fields.bodyText: For millennia, the high peaks of the Himalayas were held together by an invisible, frozen cement – permafrost and glacial ice that bound ancient rock into seemingly unshakable fortresses. But as the planet continues to warm, this alpine glue is liquefying. The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet was not a freak weather event; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. And it was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes, illustrating with a sole unnatural disaster the apocalyptic future that lies in store if we fail to take dramatic climate action. As the death toll continues to mount – the latest count showed more than 900 dead and more than 4,400 individuals missing – this event has crystalized the climate crisis for many. One reason is undoubtedly the sheer horror of what unfolded here. Chilling surveillance and eyewitness footage captured the horrific moment a 40mph wall of “liquid concrete” violently overtook fleeing crowds, instantly swallowing entire families and burying them beneath feet of thick, red-soaked silt. Another reason, however, is that the connection with climate change was unassailable in this case. The torrent was the direct result of warming-induced glacial collapse, which dumped millions of tons of rock, unleashing a high-velocity wave of mud and debris. The new reality in the era of human-caused climate change, a CNN headline put it, is that “living downstream from a glacier has become a deadly liability”. The impact of climate change on extreme weather, by contrast, is usually established though a statistical, rather than direct causal, connection. Through what is known as attribution science, climate scientists demonstrate the influence of climate change on the characteristics of an extreme weather event. It is analogous to how epidemiologists establish a linkage between cause (eg smoking cigarettes) and effect (lung cancer), through massive statistical evidence. In the case of climate attribution, scientists run parallel climate model simulations, including a “control” simulation that represents a counterfactual world without human impact, and a “treatment” simulation where human drivers – primarily the increase in greenhouse gas concentrations – are included. They then compare how often a particular event happens in the two cases. If there is a substantial increase in occurrence of a particular event in the “treatment” simulation relative to the “control” simulation, then the extremeness of the event – and its human, societal or environmental impacts – can be “attributed” to climate change. Critics might say that the connection here is merely statistical – almost circumstantial. But much as we are willing to attribute causality when a lifetime smoker contracts lung cancer because they were as much as 30 times more likely to do so because of their use of tobacco products, the extreme characteristics (unusually massive precipitation totals, high temperatures or destructive winds) of the weather event can be attributed to human-caused warming. While the tragic and deadly Tibetan flood might have been the most prominent climate change-induced disaster this summer, it followed an unprecedented series of deadly, destructive and dangerous extreme weather events that can be connected to rising carbon pollution and the warming of our planet. This summer of extremes began early. It started out with a March “heat dome” in the south-western US that yielded extremes of heat we only expect to see in mid-summer. The unprecedented extreme March heat was found by climate scientists to have been “virtually impossible” in the absence of human-caused warming. Then came a midsummer-like May heat dome in the eastern US that smashed temperature records in my home city of Philadelphia. And within weeks, a European heat dome brought deadly triple-digit temperatures to large parts of France leading to the deaths of more than 3,000 people in Paris and nearly 6,000 for all of France. That was just the first of four record-breaking, back-to-back heatwaves in Europe that, by summer’s end, has cost the lives of more than 35,000 people. And yes, the deadly heat was attributed to climate change. The record July heat combined with extreme dryness over large parts of western Europe – particularly France and Spain – to generate catastrophic wildfires that dominated the headlines for weeks, along with a viral photo of vacationers calmly lounging under a colorful umbrella while apocalyptic wildfire smoke billows in the background. The fires forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people from their homes. And at the risk of sounding like a broken record: yes, it was formally attributed to human-caused warming. Back in the US, we had our own wildfire problems. A combination of very hot and dry conditions over southern Ontario and the upper midwest led to huge wildfires generating plumes of smoke that choked the east coast for weeks. Air quality was rated hazardous in my home city of Philadelphia. And yes, these wildfires – and indeed, the Canadian wildfires we now see summer after summer – can be attributed to climate change. The summer of extreme weather disasters wasn’t done with us yet. In mid-August a historic “derecho” (a very wide, fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms associated typically with destructive, hurricane-strength straight-line destructive winds) struck the midwestern US with winds exceeding 100mph and devastating flooding, the better part of a million people from Illinois to Virginia were left without power. While it is a challenge to apply attribution methods to these rare events, there is emerging evidence that climate change is making them more frequent and more damaging. This past summer’s collective extreme weather disasters were an unmistakable consequence of the continued warming of our planet. The current administration’s policies – which were written by polluters themselves – are making things worse. Donald Trump and enabling congressional Republicans continue to double down on policies favoring fossil fuel extraction and dependence at the very time we need to be moving even more quickly away from fossil fuels toward clean energy. These extreme events underscore the urgency of taking action now, and – while there are many things we can do – one of the greatest opportunities Americans will have to affect climate policy is the upcoming midterm election. You can make support for urgent and dramatic climate action a litmus test issue as you go to the voting booth. Michael Mann is presidential distinguished professor and director of the Penn Center for Science, Sustainability and the Media at the University of Pennsylvania, and co-author with Peter Hotez, of the recent book Science Under Siege

webTitle: Afternoon Update: Australian missing in Nepal-Tibet floods found alive; Ray Hadley takes stand at Alan Jones trial; and the Kākāpō bounces back

fields.headline: Afternoon Update: Australian missing in Nepal-Tibet floods found alive; Ray Hadley takes stand at Alan Jones trial; and the Kākāpō bounces back
fields.trailText: Foreign minister ‘incredibly thankful’ another Australian has been found and says they have spoken with their family
fields.bodyText: Good afternoon. An Australian believed to be missing after floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week has been found alive. The person made contact with officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) on Tuesday from Tibet. “We’re incredibly thankful another Australian, who had been unaccounted for, has now been found,” the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said. They are receiving support from Australian consular officers and have spoken with their family. This brings down the number of Australians missing in the flash floods from 43 to 42 and comes after another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located on the weekend. Top news Rival Ray Hadley tells Alan Jones trial that alleged victim ‘broke down and sobbed’ when detailing assaults Teenager pleads guilty to planning terrorist bombing targeting Opera House and Sydney marathon China is concealing scale of flood disaster, say Tibet campaigners Kākāpō rising: 90 chicks swell population of the world’s heaviest parrot Meal deal: meth found hidden inside McMuffin during a police car search in Western Australia In video Thirty years after the killing of Tupac Shakur, one man has now been held criminally responsible for the rap icon’s death. A Las Vegas jury has found the former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of murder. A 12-person jury unanimously found Davis guilty of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, which carries a potential sentence of life in prison without parole, after nearly three hours of deliberation. You can watch the final moments of the trial here. What they said … *** “One needs to look at oneself and one’s behaviour.” – Attorney general Michelle Rowland After the Secret Harbour byelection, Anthony Albanese told Queensland Labor’s state conference that One Nation was “dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest”. In a strongly worded riposte on social media, Pauline Hanson said Albanese’s comments “crossed a line” and that “words have consequences”. “That is how political violence is incited,” she wrote. But today, Rowland suggested Hanson’s own rhetoric was also playing a role in this political landscape, saying: “I don’t wish ill on Ms Hanson in a physical way. I don’t wish any politician any ill will, irrespective of their political persuasion. But I think sometimes when comments like this are made, one needs to look at oneself and one’s behaviour and the kinds of standards that they accept into their own party and their own ideology.” Podcast Trump’s trade war with Canada gets nasty In the past couple of weeks, the Trump administration has reignited its trade war with Canada, threatened an “economic D-day” against Iran and watched the US national debt surpass $40tn. Meanwhile, Donald Trump has personally made billions of dollars since returning to office. Jonathan Freedland speaks to Dan Alexander of Forbes about how Trump has amassed his fortune – and what his economic record could mean for voters in the midterms. Listen to the episode here, and watch it on YouTube here. Before bed read Jane Davies was “drenched, freezing, utterly miserable and with a GI catastrophe ready to blow” when she dropped out of a 100km ultramarathon. Runners like Davies train for months, sometimes years. But what happens when they don’t finish a race? Daily word game Today’s starter word is: DIS. You have five goes to get the longest word including the starter word. Play Wordiply. Sign up Enjoying the Afternoon Update? Then you’ll love our Morning Mail newsletter. Sign up here to start the day with a curated breakdown of the key stories you need to know, and complete your daily news roundup. And follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland. Contact us If you have a story tip or technical issue viewing this newsletter, please reply to this email. If you are a Guardian supporter and need assistance with regards to contributions and/or digital subscriptions, please email customer.help@guardian.co.uk

webTitle: Trump’s ballroom construction can resume at White House, supreme court rules – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump’s ballroom construction can resume at White House, supreme court rules – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: The Supreme Court allowed Donald Trump to continue building his $400m White House ballroom project. In a 5-4 decision along political lines, the justices found that a group issuing a legal challenge against the ballroom did not have standing to bring their case. Trump celebrated with a post on his Truth Social platform while Democrats criticized the decision. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down from his role after 18 months on the job, leaving another top military position vacant. Driscoll and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had reportedly butted heads for some time. Trump vowed further strikes on Iran and called it a “failed nation”. The remarks came as Washington and Tehran exchanged their first military strikes in a month. JD Vance gave a speech in Michigan that included an attacked against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil,” Vance told the crowd. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney of turning their trade dispute into a “political shouting match”. Carney had rejected the Trump administration’s terms that would have given the US government extensive power over Canada’s trade policy. California Governor Gavin Newsom vowed to block the appointment of election denier Tina Peters, who was convicted in 2024 in relation to a plot to chase pro-Trump election conspiracies. Newsom announced he would take measures to prevent Peters from working as an election consultant for Northern California’s Shasta county. Former Colorado elections clerk Tina Peters, who was convicted in 2024 in relation to a plot to chase pro-Trump election conspiracies, has declined an offer to serve as an election consultant in a Northern California county, according to the Record Searchlight. Shasta County Registrar Clint Curtis caused widespread political backlash in recent weeks after he offered Peters a role as consultant, despite her election denial views and past conviction. California Governor Gavin Newsom on Monday vowed to block the hiring by instructing the state’s department of correction to reject the transfer of her parole supervision from Colorado. “Shasta County’s job offer to a felon CONVICTED OF TAMPERING WITH VOTING MACHINES to work on their election process is a disgrace,” Newsom’s press office posted on X. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down from his post after 18 months on the job and amid a wider shakeup of military leaders. Driscoll, a former Yale Law School classmate of JD Vance, submitted his resignation this week after months of tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to The Wall Street Journal. Hegseth has fired numerous top military leaders over the past year, including Army Chief of Staff Randy George. Driscoll was tasked last year with being the US government’s point person in negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in attempt to end their conflict, despite having little background in international diplomacy. He also backed incorporating more advanced technologies into the armed forces, including a push to cut down the time frame for testing new military technology. Donald Trump posted a Truth Social message on Monday evening celebrating the supreme court’s decision to allow construction to continue on his White House ballroom project. “I am pleased to report that the United States Supreme Court has just ruled in favor of the Ballroom/Military Complex being built without any further contingency, doubt, or threat,” Trump said. “We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.” The supreme court’s decision to allow Donald Trump to continue with construction of his White House found that the group suing to block it did not have standing to bring its case. The 5-4 decision, backed by the conservative justices, ruled that the National Trust for Historic Preservation did not have legal standing and had not suffered “injury in fact” from the project. Chief Justice John Roberts, joined by liberal justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, issued a dissenting opinion arguing that the court’s decision hands the presidency even more executive power and that the ballroom’s construction is likely unlawful. “The president ordered the demolition of the East Wing of the White House to make way for a new, privately funded state ballroom in its place. Construction of the ballroom has proceeded apace for the better part of a year,” Chief Justice John Roberts wrote in a dissent. “That construction is likely unlawful”. The Supreme Court issued a decision on Monday that gives Donald Trump the ability to proceed with his plans for construction of a new White House ballroom. Trump’s plans for a White House ballroom have been an ongoing point of contention and legal action, with opponents arguing that Trump has no legal authority to pursue the project without congressional approval. In a 5-4 decision, the court granted the Trump administration’s request to block a lower court ruling that would have prevented work from being done on the ballroom. The Supreme Court also issued a temporary order earlier this month which allowed work to continue on the ballroom, resulting in Democratic Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer accusing the court of “rubber stamping Trump’s vanity-driven, gilded corruption”. In the Oval Office today, Donald Trump said the latest strikes on Iran, as the two countries exchange fire for the first time in a month, are part of a “limited” campaign. “They’re a failed nation,” the president said after threatening to hit “Iran” hard after the regime struck Jordanian airbases over the weekend. “Their leaders are largely dead. Their navy is gone. Their air force is gone,” Trump told reporters today. “That doesn’t mean we won’t smack them. We’ll see what happens.” The president also claimed that traffic is increasing through the vital strait of Hormuz chokepoint, even though the average number is substantially lower – and has remained so – since the war began. There was, however, an uptick in the number of transits in the past two weeks, before the most recent strikes. Chris Hippensteel Vance – who has now finished speaking in Michigan – also fired back at El-Sayed for comments the Democratic nominee made about Vance’s wife on social media. “Abdul, keep my wife’s name the hell out of your mouth because she’s way out of your league,” Vance told the crowd. El-Sayed had previously insinuated in a post that Vance would not have introduced his wife, Usha, to his late grandfather, a remark that was widely interpreted as jab at Usha Vance’s Indian-American heritage. Donald Trump is now speaking in the Oval Office about price cuts for prescription drugs. We’ll bring you the latest lines. Chris Hippensteel JD Vance has turned his address in Michigan toward Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Mike Rogers’ Democratic opponent in Michigan’s Senate race. The vice-president is taking aim at El-Sayed’s association with leftwing political commentator Hasan Piker, and for comments El-Sayed made after an attack on the Temple Israel synagogue in West Bloomfield, Michigan, in March. El-Sayed has apologized for those comments, saying they were meant to add context. At the time the nominee condemned the violence but added that “hurt people hurt people” and that “violence is a cycle”. “I made a mistake,” El-Sayed said over the weekend at an event in Lansing, and apologized for his comments. “If my statement caused pain, I’m sorry,” he added. “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil,” Vance said today, describing El-Sayed as divisive and as willing to pit racial and religious groups against one another. Trump vowed further strikes on Iran after a series of ballistic missile attacks on US airbases in Jordan. “We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told a Fox News correspondent, adding: “There will be a response.” Iran fired ballistic missiles at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan after the US launched its own strike on Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday night, the first US strikes on the country in more than a month. Larak Island is located near the mouth of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway and oil shipping chokepoint which has been at the center of the conflict. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent delivered opening remarks at a G20 meeting while touting the Trump administration’s new Iran sanctions. Bessent – who used his opening remarks at the conference of world financial leaders to praise President Trump – faces the challenge of winning the support of allies and adversaries for a plan to further isolate Iran’s already war-battered economy. He started off by thanking the EU for backing that plan. Speaking to the media before and after those opening remarks, Bessent expressed optimism that the sanctions could force Iran’s leaders to make a deal. He also spoke dismissively of Canada’s efforts to retaliate against the US in the two nations’ escalating trade showdown. Trump decried datacenter opposition on Truth Social on Monday. As a movement opposing the breakneck buildout of datacenters across the country gains steam, Trump took to his personal social media platform to scold those who want to see construction of the facilities slowed or put to a halt. The only reason communities would speak out against datacenters is “if they want to end up being backwards and poor”, Trump wrote. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he added. The House of Representatives returned from a recess on Monday, with Republicans eager to avoid a shutdown. After a five-week hiatus, House Republicans are seeking to push through a stopgap spending bill to stave off a government shutdown, after multiple full or partial federal shutdowns have snarled Congress since the start of the second Trump administration. Funding is currently secured through the end of September, and GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson is expected to hold a floor vote on the issue this week. Chris Hippensteel Vice-president JD Vance has taken the stage in Sterling Heights, Michigan, at a campaign event supporting Republican candidates up for election in the state in November. He opened his remarks to the crowd by focusing on illegal immigration, and American workers – particularly American truck drivers – he describes as being displaced by undocumented immigrants. “American jobs ought to go to American workers, not illegal foreigners,” Vance said. Providers are seeing more patients in need of abortions later in pregnancy as abortion bans and restrictions proliferate in US states, all while access to insurance falls. Those bans and restrictions have also meant that later abortion care access has grown over the past decade in a handful of haven states and cities. Patients are showing up “later and sicker” in need of reproductive healthcare, said Diane Horvath, a co-founder of Partners in Abortion Care in Maryland. About 41 states have abortion bans or significant restrictions at some point in pregnancy. More than 20 million people have lost Medicaid coverage since 2023, while between 3 and 5 million people have lost or dropped their coverage through Affordable Care Act exchanges in recent months. “People are getting chucked off of Medicaid. The premiums are all going up,” Horvath said. Instead of seeking care early in pregnancy, she said: “They’re just not going in. There’s no place to go.” The cost of later abortion – which is loosely defined as anything past the first trimester, the time during which the vast majority of abortions occur – tends to rise the later it happens in a pregnancy. “Sometimes you’re looking at a $22,000 gap with maybe three days to pull together funding,” said Alisha Dingus, executive director of the DC Abortion Fund (DCAF), one of the largest abortion funds in the country. Rising costs and decreasing availability “may create substantial barriers to accessing later abortion care”, a recent Jama study found. Read the full report here: As we reported earlier, the United States and Iran have exchanged fire for the first time in a month, with missiles and drones fired at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, and Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan and the UAE in response. Donald Trump has threatened further action. Here’s my colleague Patrick Wintour’s report: Vice-president JD Vance will shortly be speaking at a manufacturing facility in Sterling Heights, Michigan. He is there campaigning on behalf of several Republican nominees in key statewide races, including Mike Rogers, who is running for Senate in a closely watched race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, and congressman John James, who is running to replace Gretchen Whitmer in the governor’s race. James will face Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, in the November general election. I’ll bring you all the key lines from Vance’s remarks when it gets going. Pete Hegseth regularly receives formal objections from senior commanders and proceeds anyway, the Pentagon’s top spokesman has said, as he tried to discredit a Washington Post report that four generals and admirals had advised against prolonging the war against Iran. “Of course, we demand candid military advice,” Sean Parnell wrote on X. “Non-concurs are standard. The Secretary sees them constantly. That’s how you run a real military.” Parnell was responding to the Post’s account of four four-star commanders who had lodged formal “non-concurs” against a plan to keep more than 50,000 US troops in the Middle East through September, with some deployments potentially running into 2027. In dismissing the story, Parnell did not dispute that the objections had been filed, or that Hegseth fields such dissent on an ongoing basis. “Publishing highly classified assessments from the Secretary’s orders book is a crime,” he wrote. “It’s a betrayal of the force. And much of what they’re publishing is inaccurate … We are in great shape around the world. This story isn’t about readiness. It’s TDS and PDS – they hate President Trump and Secretary Hegseth more than they love America.” It was unclear which parts of the story the Pentagon deems to be inaccurate. A community note attached to the X post noted that, while leaking classified material is illegal for government employees, the US supreme court ruled in 1971 that the first amendment protects the press’s right to publish classified information of public interest. Here’s Joseph’s full report: Prediction market platform Kalshi has issued its first lifetime ban on none other than the disgraced former Republican congressman George Santos, who bet against his own announced plans to attend Donald Trump’s State of the Union address. In a filing, Kalshi said of the affair: “The Compliance Department found that Santos made these statements with the intent to manipulate the price of the Yes or No contracts that he intended to purchase. Ultimately, these statements did in fact manipulate the price of said contracts. “The Compliance Department has issued a penalty permanently suspending Santos from direct or indirect access to Kalshi and has imposed a penalty of $71,356.” The company said he had made $17,839.57 from his wagers. Santos responded in a post on X this morning: “Hey @Kalshi thanks for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform. Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for.” Santos was released from prison in New Jersey in October after Donald Trump commuted his seven-year, three-month sentence for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. The former congressman was revealed to have fabricated much about his life during his congressional campaign and was expelled from Congress while under federal investigation for fraud in 2023. Following his release, Santos returned to X in February to tell his millions of followers that he planned to attend Trump’s speech. “I’m gonna be in the gallery,” he wrote. But he didn’t attend the event. “I guess people lost money,” he said on his podcast in March. “Some people made unexpected money. That’s to show you how fragile these markets are.” He was also fined $35,000 and received a three-year trading ban from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission last month for alleged market manipulation over the incident. Vance also said that Trump was sending a message ⁠to Iran ⁠with his AI-generated social media video, posted over the weekend, that shows the US bombing ⁠Kharg Island. “The president ‌likes to ‌switch it up ‌on social media a little bit. He would be the first to ‌say he doesn’t make announcements about military actions on social media, but I think that he’s ⁠sending a message to the Iranians,” Vance said when asked about ‌Trump’s post. A US ‌official said on Monday the military had not targeted Kharg Island in overnight strikes. An Iranian official dismissed Trump’s post as “laughable”. Speaking to reporters before he took off for Detroit, JD Vance defended the Donald Trump’s earlier comments about Americans who oppose datacenter construction, but attempted to underscore the need for tech companies to subsidize the higher energy costs that come with the AI expansion. “I think probably 99% of the backlash to datacenters has come in areas where building a datacenter means higher utility and higher electricity for the people on the ground,” Vance said. “If you build a datacenter – you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out. And if that is happening, I don’t think the datacenters are that controversial. It’s when the utility bills get so much higher that’s when it’s a real problem.” Chris Hippensteel Bessent also briefly touched on the new Iran sanctions earlier this morning, before his opening remarks in Asheville. Speaking to reporters, Bessent predicted that, under the latest round of sanctions, Iran’s economy could collapse within “weeks or months”. But he also suggested that a deal, not collapse, was the administration’s primary goal. “The economy doesn’t have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses,” Bessent said. Chris Hippensteel Asked on CNBC about the escalating US-Canada trade war with Canada, Bessent spoke dismissively of Canada’s ability to economically retaliate against US tariffs. “I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone 13 times larger than you are,” Bessent said. He also accused Canadian prime minister Mark Carney of turning a trade dispute into “a political shouting match”. This comes after Donald Trump signed an executive order ordering the US interior department to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” in response to the back-and-forth of tariffs between the two countries. “[Carney] is doing what’s best for the Liberal party, what’s best for Mark Carney. And in the long run, the Canadian people are going to see through that,” Bessent said today. “They were offered the best trade deal of any country on the globe,” Bessent added, “and he chose to walk away from it at the last minute.” In another Truth Social missive today, Donald Trump has taken aim at the Americans who oppose the construction of datacenters – the power-demanding warehouses that tech companies use to house their computer servers and systems. The president said that the “only reason” communities would not want datacenters is “if they want to end up being backwards and poor”. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” Trump wrote. “The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.” Across the country anti-datacenter animus has galvanized many areas – both Democratic and Republican. According to recent polling, 75% of Americans oppose a new datacenter being built near where they live. Meanwhile, more than a dozen states have weighed temporary bans on new datacenter construction, and New York last month became the first to enact one. Progressive stalwarts Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio‑Cortez are now pushing for a national moratorium. And in Texas, even Governor Greg Abbott – a hard‑right Republican – has called for halting datacenter development in rural parts of the state. Trump, for his part, is politically boxed in: he’s pushing to make the US a leader in artificial‑intelligence innovation – a goal that depends on rapid datacenter expansion – while also promising to bring down electricity costs for consumers, who are already facing higher bills. “China could not be happier with this anti‑Data Center movement,” Trump wrote in a social‑media post. “Actually, they can’t believe it is happening!” As my colleague, Dharna Noor has reported, so far the president’s answer to this bind is the “Ratepayer Protection Pledge” – a voluntary agreement he says will prevent families from paying for the AI boom. Nearly 200 companies, utilities, datacenter developers and states have signed on, the administration announced last month. But several environmental groups have dismissed the pledge as “toothless”, noting that it carries no legal force. Chris Hippensteel Scott Bessent told CNBC that he’d met the previous night with Pan Gongsheng, the governor of China’s central bank. Their meeting – of which Bessent revealed few details – came amid speculation that the US would struggle to successfully isolate Iran under its latest sanctions without buy-in from China. Bessent pushed back on those criticisms during his CNBC interview. He said that the US and China are largely aligned on their goals for Iran, including reopening the strait of Hormuz and keeping nuclear weapons out of the regime’s hands. But he also argued that the US could succeed in crippling Iran’s economy with or without China’s cooperation. The treasury secretary declined to share details of his conversation with Pan Gongsheng, or to speak in any depth about what direction the US and China are trending in – be it toward cooperation or standoff – behind closed doors. Chris Hippensteel Speaking with CNBC after his opening remarks in Asheville, Bessent said that the goal of the latest round of sanctions on Iran was to force the Iranian regime to the negotiating table. Pressed on whether the hardline Iranian leadership could be moved by the economic strangulation of its people, Bessent appeared to suggest that the threat of popular uprising in response to those conditions might motivate the regime to make a deal. “The main thing they care about is their head staying attached to their neck,” Bessent said. Donald Trump previously expressed hope that the US’s initial strike on Iran, which killed the nation’s ageing supreme leader, would prompt such a revolt. That prediction has, so far, not come to pass. Today we’ll also be tracking vice-president JD Vance’s trip to Detroit, Michigan, where he’ll be speaking at a manufacturing facility and campaigning on behalf of several Republican nominees in key statewide races. This includes Mike Rogers, who is running for Senate in a closely watched race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, and John James, a congressman who is running to replace Gretchen Whitmer in the governor’s race. James will face Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, in the November general election. Kevin Warsh, speaking briefly after Bessent in Asheville, described the current global financial landscape as one of surging investment and growth – with little mention of the headwinds facing the economy. “The future is already here, but we’re all experiencing it somewhat different,” the new Federal Reserve chair said. Last week at the Jackson Hole symposium, Warsh did not indicate where the Fed will take interest rates in the coming months, despite US inflation remaining stubbornly above the central bank’s 2% target amid the war in Iran. Donald Trump has told Fox News’s chief foreign correspondent, Trey Yingst, that the US will respond to Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan overnight. “We’re going to hit them hard,” Trump told Fox News. “There will be a response,” he added, after Jordan’s army confirmed it had intercepted eight missiles early this morning. In response to the US assault on Larak Island late on Sunday, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV. In the interview with Fox News on Monday, Trump said all of the missiles were intercepted by American air defence systems, except one which was allowed to pass through the airspace because it was identified as not on course to hit anything “significant”, according to Yingst. Chris Hippensteel Before turning the microphone over to Kevin Warsh, Bessent thanked the European Union and the European Central Bank for their support of US plans to further isolate Iran from the global economy. That plan – dubbed Operation Economic Outcast – requires the US to win the cooperation of allies and adversaries alike, with a threat of punishment to states and companies that continue to do business with the regime. Bessent said, without offering specifics, that the plan would lead to the toppling of the Iranian leadership, a goal that the Trump administration has been vowing to bring about since the war’s opening days. Chris Hippensteel Bessent opened his remarks by pointing to the host city of Asheville, North Carolina, as a beacon of economic recovery in the aftermath of Hurricane Helene, before promptly pivoting to praise for Trump. “Under President Trump, we are entering a new season of national strength,” Bessent told the assembled global leaders. Bessent criticized the G20 as having lost its founding priorities in fostering economic growth, and said Trump was bringing the G20 back to that original purpose. Chris Hippensteel We’re watching today as Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, and Kevin Warsh, the chair of the Federal Reserve, deliver their opening remarks at the G20 meetings in Asheville, North Carolina. The meetings are unfolding in the shadow of economic disruptions downstream of the war in Iran, which has choked global energy markets and driven up inflation around the world. Bessent is speaking first. The US House is back after a five-week recess. And this week, Republicans are focused a key legislative agenda item: passing a stopgap spending bill to stave off a possible government shutdown. Currently, funding is guaranteed through 30 September, but after a year marked by record-breaking shutdowns, GOP House speaker Mike Johnson is hoping to advance a bill that would extend funding spending at its current levels until after the November midterms. Johnson is expected to put a vote on the House floor this week, using a fast-track procedure that requires a two-thirds majority to pass. Prior to the Senate heading home for their August recess, the upper chamber approved its own continuing resolution to keep the government until 11 December, this also included provisions like preventing political appointees having approvals over federal grants. The House is set to leave Washington again at the end of this week for Labor Day recess, provided it can get through its to-do list. Donald Trump has claimed that Iran is a “Failed Nation” and that the regime is “DEAD” in a post on Truth Social today. This comes as Washington and Tehran exchange their first strikes in a month, after the US struck Larak Island in the strait of Hormuz, and Iran retaliated by targeting Jordanian airbases. Trump, however, insisted that the country’s economic condition had rendered them powerless. “They have no currency,” the president said, after the Iranian rial dropped to a record low last week. “They are not paying their soldiers or police, Inflation is at 300%, and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country.” Trump added that “the only thing” Iran has is “FAKE NEWS from the USA, a willingness to kill their protesters (now over 100,000 people dead. They must be tried for war crimes against humanity!), and a good line of “BULLSHIT”. It’s worth noting that US prices are up 3.4% compared with a year ago in the US. The average price for gallon of fuel is also a dollar higher than this time last year, before the war with Iran started. My colleagues are covering the latest developments out of the Middle East: Donald Trump is in Washington today. He’ll begin his day in closed-door meetings, but we’ll hear from the president at 3pm ET in the Oval Office, when he makes an announcement on healthcare affordability and prescription drug pricing. We’ll bring you the latest lines as that gets under way. The White House “border czar,” Tom Homan, denied on Sunday that deporting British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos just a day after being arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) amounted to preferential treatment. Homan said it was his understanding that Yiannopoulos, 41, had overstayed what he believed to be a visitor visa, had not appeared at an immigration hearing and was issued a final order of removal on 22 July. “He didn’t show up,” Homan told CNN’s State of the Union. “The judge ordered him deported. So, once ICE gets an order of deportation from a federal judge, their job is to execute that order, and that’s what they did.” He added: “He had his due process, ordered removed by a federal judge, and ICE removed him. It’s that simple.” Yiannopoulos’s removal one day after his arrest, when many others who have been deported had first endured lengthy detention center incarcerations, has prompted questions about whether he received preferential treatment in that respect.
